records.text: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are a cornerstone of the deep learning revolution.
The design of CNNs was partly inspired by the structure of the mammalian visual cortex.
The seminal work by Hubel and Wiesel revealed how the brain processes visual information through a hierarchy of simple feature detectors.
Hubel and Wiesel received the Nobel Prize for these studies.
Hubel and Wiesel's key experimental breakthrough was the ability to fabricate micro-electrodes fine enough to record the activity of a single neuron in a living brain.
The brain used in these experiments was often that of a cat.
Using these micro-electrodes, Hubel and Wiesel discovered that neurons in the very first processing stage (the primary visual cortex, V1) do not see the whole image.
Each neuron in V1 has a small receptive field.
Each neuron in V1 responds only to extremely simple patterns inside its receptive field.
For instance, a neuron in V1 might fire intensely for a bright vertical line.
The same neuron becomes almost silent as the line is rotated.
The observed properties of V1 neurons suggest a hierarchical organisation where the first layer extracts local primitives (edges, orientations).
In this hierarchical organisation, a second layer would combine these primitives into more complex shapes (e.g., a corner from a horizontal and a vertical line).
Hubel and Wiesel did identify neurons in the second visual area (V2) that responded to combinations of primitives (e.g., corners from horizontal and vertical lines).
Hubel and Wiesel wisely stopped at identifying V2 neurons; they did not claim to understand the full visual cortex hierarchy.
The true structure of the visual cortex is immensely more complicated than a simple hierarchy.
A simplified picture of the visual cortex shows a sequence of layers: V1 → V2 → V3 → V4 → V5/V6.
In reality, the visual cortex is a dense mesh of feed-forward, feedback and lateral connections.
The biological brain is not a clean feed-forward network.
A single biological neuron has exactly one output: its axon.
To perform gradient descent, every node in a computational graph must implement at least a forward computation and a backward gradient computation.
Implementing both forward and backward gradient computation is fundamentally impossible for a single biological neuron.
Therefore, the human brain cannot train itself by gradient descent.
The human brain must rely on massive feedback loops and a different, still unknown learning mechanism.

The analogy between artificial and biological neurons stops at the connectionist principle (a large composition of simple units can yield complex behaviour) and at the layered hierarchical organisation.
Nevertheless, the observed hierarchy of simple-to-complex features in the visual cortex was the conceptual seed for convolutional networks.
Building on the inspiration from the visual cortex hierarchy, Kunihiko Fukushima proposed the Neocognitron in 1979.
The Neocognitron was a deep, multi-layer architecture that used fixed filters (convolutions) to extract features across an image.
The Neocognitron employed activations very similar to modern ReLU (the hinge-shaped activation) decades before ReLU became standard.
The Neocognitron lacked learning; its filters were hand-designed, not trained.
Convolutional networks in their modern, trainable form were developed in the late 1980s by Yann LeCun and his group.
Yann LeCun's key contribution was making the convolution kernels learnable via backpropagation.
Yann LeCun's architectures (such as LeNet) demonstrated the power of learnable convolution kernels on practical tasks like handwritten digit recognition.
The fundamental assumption behind CNNs is translation invariance of feature detectors.
Translation invariance means that if you are looking for a specific pattern (e.g., a boy's face, a digit, a corner), exactly the same detector should be applied everywhere across the image.
The location of a pattern changes the input, but the function that detects the pattern remains identical.
The translation invariance assumption leads to a specific pipeline in CNNs.
In the CNN pipeline, the input (an image, or any multi-dimensional array) is divided into small, overlapping windows (tiles).
Typically odd-sized tiles such as 3x3 or 5x5 are used.
In the CNN pipeline, a small neural network (in practice just a single fully-connected layer) is applied to every tile.
This small neural network receives the tile's pixel values (flattened into a vector) and outputs a vector of new features.
Because each tile yields a feature vector and the tiles form a spatial grid, the output of a convolutional layer is a three-dimensional tensor of dimensions height × width × number of features.
The number of features is often called channels or feature maps.
The spatial dimensions of the output tensor may shrink unless special measures like padding are taken.
The process of convolution can be repeated: the output tensor of one layer becomes the input of the next layer, which again is tiled, processed with a new small network, and so on.
By stacking convolution layers, the network builds a hierarchy of features, from simple edges to complex shapes.
The crucial gain of convolutional layers is weight sharing: the same small weight matrix is reused for every tile.
Weight sharing means that the number of trainable parameters does not depend on the size of the input image, only on the tile (kernel) size and the number of input/output channels.
Weight sharing drastically reduces the number of parameters compared to a fully-connected layer.
Weight sharing acts as a powerful structural regulariser.
Weight sharing encodes the prior knowledge of translation invariance by explicitly imposing that the same operation must be performed everywhere.
A drawback of stacking only convolutional layers is that the receptive field grows very slowly.
With 3x3 kernels, each convolutional layer adds only 2 pixels to the effective field of view.
To reach a receptive field covering a 256x256 image, about 130 convolutional layers would be needed, which is impractical.
Therefore, classical CNNs introduce pooling layers to aggressively reduce the spatial dimensions.
A pooling layer operates on the output of a convolutional layer.
A pooling layer partitions the feature maps into small, non-overlapping windows, almost always 2x2.
For each 2x2 window, the pooling layer replaces the four values with a single summary statistic.
In max-pooling, the summary statistic is the maximum of the four values.
In average-pooling, the summary statistic is the mean of the four values.
Max-pooling is overwhelmingly the standard choice in CNNs.
For "presence" features such as whether a face, a corner, or an edge is present, the maximum across the window is the correct composition.
If any tile in the window detects the object, the whole window should report its presence.
Average-pooling tends to dilute strong presence signals.
Features that measure continuous quantities (e.g., colour saturation) may benefit from averaging.
Object-oriented features obey the max law.
Empirically, max-pooling works better than average-pooling.
With 2x2 pooling, the width and height of the feature maps are halved, reducing the number of features by a factor of four.
Pooling layers have zero trainable parameters.
Pooling layers are deterministic down-sampling operations.
Let x^l be the input feature map at layer l, with spatial dimensions and depth D.
A two-dimensional convolution uses a kernel of size (2d+1)x(2d+1).
The weight tensor W for a convolution has shape (2d+1)x(2d+1)x D x D', where D' is the desired number of output features.
For each output position (i,j) and each output channel c', the convolution operation is: y^l_{i,j,c'} = \sum_{c=1}^{D} \sum_{-d \le a,b \le d} W_{a,b,c,c'} x^l_{i+a, j+b, c}.

In simpler notation, the per-channel convolution is written as: y^l_{i,j} = \sum_{-d \le a,b \le d} W_{a,b} x^l_{i+a, j+b}, implicitly summing over input channels and using a separate kernel for each output channel.
After the convolution, a nonlinearity is applied element-wise: z^l_{i,j} = h(y^l_{i,j}).
In almost all modern CNNs, the nonlinearity h is the ReLU function: h(u) = \max(0,u).
Max-pooling over a (2d+1)x(2d+1) window is defined as: x^{l+1}_{i,j} = \max_{-d \le a,b \le d} z^l_{i+a, j+b}.
Average-pooling replaces the maximum with the arithmetic mean in the pooling operation.
After several convolution-pooling blocks, the spatial dimensions become small enough that the whole tensor can be flattened and fed into one or more fully-connected layers (the classification head).
To appreciate the parameter savings, consider a classical LeNet-style network for grayscale 32x32 input (depth 1).
The architecture of this LeNet-style network proceeds in a specific sequence of layers.
Input: 1 x 32 x 32.
Conv1: 5x5 kernel, 6 output features → output 6 x 28 x 28.
Conv1 has weights: 1 x 5 x 5 x 6 = 150.
Max-pooling1: 2x2 → output 6 x 14 x 14.
Max-pooling1 has 0 weights because it is deterministic.
Conv2: 5x5 kernel, 16 output features → output 16 x 10 x 10.
Conv2 has weights: 6 x 5 x 5 x 16 = 2400.
Max-pooling2: 2x2 → output 16 x 5 x 5.
Max-pooling2 has 0 weights.
Fully-connected 1: The 16x5x5 = 400 values are flattened and mapped to 120 neurons.
Fully-connected 1 weights: 400 x 120 = 48,000 (plus biases).
Fully-connected 2: 120 → 84.
Fully-connected 2 weights: 120 x 84 = 10,080.
Output (softmax) layer: 84 → 10.
Output layer weights: 84 x 10 = 840.
Total trainable parameters ≈ 150 + 2400 + 48,000 + 10,080 + 840 ≈ 61,470.
Of these 61,470 total trainable parameters, only about 2,550 (roughly 4%) belong to the convolutional layers.
Had the first layer been a naive fully-connected transformation from 32x32 = 1024 pixels to a 28x28x6 output, it would have required around five million weights.
The convolutional structure slashes the first layer's parameter count from around five million to 150.
This parameter reduction directly encodes the intuition that a feature detector should be location independent.
This is structural regularisation—hard-coding equality constraints on weights.
Structural regularisation is the primary reason CNNs can scale to high-resolution images.
In a CNN, every weight in the kernel is reused across every spatial tile.
In the backward pass, the gradient for a kernel weight is the sum (by the chain rule) of all the individual gradients from each tile in which that weight participates.
In a CNN, a single weight receives gradient information from the entire image.
The fact that a single weight receives gradient information from the entire image makes optimisation extremely stable.
The abundance of gradient signal points makes sparsity desirable.
With ReLU activations, many neurons output exactly zero for a given input window.
A zero ReLU activation stops gradient flow through that part of the graph for that tile.
However, the kernel weight still receives updates from all the other tiles where the activation was positive.
Sparsity accelerates computation without harming learning.
Sparsity acts as a mild regulariser.
ReLU and convolutional weight sharing are an exceptionally well-matched pair.
Applying a K x K convolution reduces the spatial dimensions by K-1.
This reduction occurs because border pixels cannot serve as the centre of a full window.
To preserve the spatial size (often desired when stacking many layers), the input can be padded with extra values before the convolution.
The two most common padding strategies are zero padding and mirror padding.
Zero padding fills out-of-bounds values with 0.
Mirror padding reflects the border pixels outward.
Zero padding sometimes creates artefacts near the border because windows near the border see many zeros.
Mirror padding mitigates border artefacts but is slightly more expensive.
The main goal of padding is to let every original pixel be the centre of a window, so that the output has the same height and width as the input.
Instead of a pooling layer, one can reduce spatial dimensions by using a stride (skipping pixels when placing windows).
If windows are centred only on every second pixel (stride 2), the number of tiles is halved in each direction, and the output dimensions become roughly W/2 x H/2.
With stride 2, no information is lost because every pixel is still covered by at least one window (often by two).
Stride 2 gives the same geometric down-sampling as a 2x2 pooling layer, but without an explicit separate pooling operation.
The stride can be set independently for height and width (a pair of numbers).
Usually, the stride is the same in both directions.
While pooling was standard in early CNNs, it has undesirable side-effects.
Pooling eliminates many computational paths.
Pooling can distort gradients.
Modern architectures such as Inception and ResNet tend to replace explicit pooling with strided convolutions or small sub-networks.
These strided convolutions or sub-networks accomplish spatial reduction while learning the best way to combine features.
Pooling is far from obsolete.
The trend is to let the network learn its own down-sampling rather than imposing a fixed max or average pooling operation.
